title: Make Them Want to Follow You: The Law of Fickleness

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Greene uses Queen Elizabeth I because leadership becomes easier to understand when a ruler has to survive unstable admiration and resentment at once. With William Cecil helping preserve form, Elizabeth kept authority from becoming too familiar. Mary Queen of Scots gives the contrast by showing how exposed, entangled authority becomes easier to test.

That is the law of fickleness. People want leadership, but their feelings toward leaders shift quickly. They admire strength, then tire of it, then probe for weakness when authority looks needy or too available. Greene's point is not that leaders should become cold. It is that followership is unstable. If a leader keeps bargaining for approval, overexplaining every move, or letting favoritism become visible, authority loses weight. Leadership lasts better when distance, steadiness, and symbolic form keep the crowd from feeling that it fully owns the leader.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Queen Elizabeth I matters here because the chapter needs a leader who understood how unstable followers can be. William Cecil helped maintain that authority, while Mary Queen of Scots shows what happens when power becomes too exposed, too personal, and too easy for others to read.

That is the law of fickleness. People say they want strong leadership, but they keep changing their emotional price on the leader. They admire authority, resent it, test it, and downgrade it fast when it starts chasing affection. Greene is not telling the reader to become icy. He is saying that followership is volatile. A leader who keeps asking to be liked, showing dependence on favorites, or answering every challenge with more explanation makes authority cheap. People trust the role more when it is not begging for reassurance. Distance, steadiness, and a little symbolic weight help leadership survive the crowd's changing mood.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Greene uses Queen Elizabeth I because she understood that followers do not stay emotionally priced the same for long. Cecil helped protect that authority. Mary Queen of Scots serves as the warning: once power looks too exposed and too personal, people start testing it harder.

The mistake is treating approval like proof of strength. Once a leader becomes too available, too eager to explain, or visibly dependent on favorites, the room senses weakness and starts repricing. Respect erodes when followers feel the role needs them. Greene is not selling coldness. He is selling authority that does not beg. Leaders forget that quickly. Distance, steadiness, and controlled appearances keep leadership from becoming emotionally cheap in a volatile field.

Greene uses Queen Elizabeth I because the problem of authority becomes clearest when a leader has to survive unstable admiration, dependence, envy, and resentment all at the same time. Elizabeth's court was not a setting of fixed loyalty. It was a field of shifting feeling. William Cecil matters because he helped keep authority in a form that could survive those shifts. Mary Queen of Scots matters because she gives the counterexample: leadership made too exposed, too personal, and too easy for others to test.

That is the law of fickleness. People want leadership, but they do not stay emotionally fixed toward leaders for very long. They admire strength, then chafe under it, then probe it when it looks needy or too available. The same followers can praise a leader one week and quietly downgrade that person the next.

This is why Greene keeps authority separate from approval. A leader can be loved at moments, but leadership becomes weaker when it depends on being continually liked. The effort to make authority feel emotionally safe and familiar can remove the very weight that makes followership steadier.

Elizabeth matters because she protected symbolic distance. She controlled access, kept her role larger than daily emotion, and did not let others feel they fully possessed her. Cecil matters because he understood that power loses force when it becomes too ordinary to the people surrounding it. Form mattered as much as warmth.

Mary Queen of Scots gives Greene the practical warning. Visible dependence on favorites, too much personal exposure, and reactive inconsistency make leadership easier to read and easier to test. Once people see where authority is hungry, they begin applying pressure there.

That is why overfamiliarity is more dangerous than it first looks. It does not merely make a leader seem warm. It can teach followers to treat authority as endlessly negotiable. Constant explanation, visible bids for approval, and obvious favoritism shift attention away from the mission and toward the leader's emotional needs.

Greene is not arguing for cold theater or inhuman remoteness. Authority without substance and steadiness eventually fails too. The point is narrower and harder: leadership needs enough form, distance, and consistency that followers do not start treating the role like a mood-managed friendship. People often claim they want authenticity, but they quickly test leaders who make power too emotionally available.

From there, every reassurance bid teaches followers that persistence matters more than the office itself. Pressure keeps coming once authority looks emotionally negotiable. It rarely stops itself.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: In the next day, notice one place where you lead and write down one way you could make the role a little steadier and less approval-dependent.
twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: Within twenty-four hours, catch one moment where you overexplain, overexpose, or show favoritism and interrupt it.
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: Today, find one point where you are discounting authority and stop doing it.

weeklyPractice.gentle: Once this week, make one leadership decision without trying to buy immediate warmth from the group afterward.
weeklyPractice.direct: At the end of the week, review one role for approval-seeking, favoritism, and unnecessary exposure.
weeklyPractice.competitive: Run one weekly authority audit and remove one cheapening habit.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: Fickleness is the instability of followership. Greene uses Queen Elizabeth I, William Cecil, and Mary Queen of Scots to show that people want leadership but quickly test it when authority becomes too familiar, too exposed, or too dependent on approval.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: The chapter teaches that popularity and authority are different assets. Leadership stays stronger when it has steadiness, distance, and symbolic weight instead of constant emotional bargaining with followers.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: Followers reprice leaders fast. If authority starts asking the room to like it, protect it, or reassure it, the role gets cheaper, favoritism starts leaking price, and hidden resentment has more room to organize.

front.gentle: What is fickleness in this law?
front.direct: What problem is Greene naming here?
front.competitive: What keeps happening to authority in this chapter?

back.gentle: Fickleness is the instability of followers' feelings toward leaders.
back.direct: People keep changing their emotional valuation of authority.
back.competitive: The field keeps repricing the leader.

front.gentle: Why does Greene use Queen Elizabeth I, William Cecil, and Mary Queen of Scots?
front.direct: What does the anchor set show?
front.competitive: Why start with these rulers and adviser figures?

back.gentle: They show preserved authority against authority made too exposed and testable.
back.direct: Elizabeth and Cecil anchor steadier leadership, while Mary sharpens the warning about vulnerable authority.
back.competitive: The set shows how power holds price or leaks it.

front.gentle: Why are popularity and authority not the same asset?
front.direct: Why can chasing approval weaken leadership?
front.competitive: Why does warmth not equal price?

back.gentle: A leader can be liked without making the role emotionally cheap.
back.direct: Authority weakens when it depends on followers for constant reassurance.
back.competitive: Once the room feels the bid for affection, it starts pushing harder.

front.gentle: What practical signs suggest authority is weakening under fickleness?
front.direct: How can you tell the role is becoming too exposed?
front.competitive: What does cheapening leadership look like in practice?

back.gentle: Overfamiliarity, favoritism, and constant explanation are common signs.
back.direct: Followers start tracking mood, access, and the leader's need for approval.
back.competitive: The room starts pricing leverage instead of mission.

front.gentle: Why does this chapter lead into aggression next?
front.direct: What hidden problem appears after unstable followership is understood?
front.competitive: Why does Greene move from fickleness to hostility behind friendly surfaces?

back.gentle: Because unstable loyalty often stores resentment before it becomes openly hostile.
back.direct: The next law studies the aggression that can remain hidden while followers are still outwardly compliant.
back.competitive: The repricing starts before the attack shows itself.

questions.prompt: What is fickleness in this law?
choices: A leader's refusal to listen to feedback
The instability of followers' feelings toward leaders
A general dislike of all authority figures

explanation.gentle: The chapter is about shifting loyalties and emotions around leadership.
explanation.direct: Followers keep changing how they feel about authority.
explanation.competitive: The field keeps repricing the role.

questions.prompt: Why does Greene use Queen Elizabeth I in this chapter?
choices: To show authority preserved through distance, form, and steadiness
To prove that leaders should reveal every private feeling
To argue that popularity is more important than leadership

explanation.gentle: Elizabeth anchors the stronger version of authority in the chapter.
explanation.direct: She shows leadership that does not become emotionally cheap.

questions.prompt: What role do William Cecil and Mary Queen of Scots play in the chapter's logic?
choices: They prove that leadership is mostly luck
They show that followers never test authority
They sharpen the contrast between steadier authority and authority made more vulnerable

explanation.gentle: The chapter uses them to make the law more concrete and comparative.
explanation.direct: Cecil supports preserved form, while Mary sharpens the warning about exposed authority.
explanation.competitive: One helps hold price and the other reveals leakage.

questions.prompt: A manager keeps reopening decisions because the team looks briefly unhappy each time. Which reading best fits the chapter?
choices: The manager is increasing authority by staying emotionally available
The manager may be making leadership more negotiable and therefore weaker
The manager has solved fickleness by giving everyone more input

explanation.gentle: Repeated reopening can teach the group to test the role more often.
explanation.direct: Approval-seeking usually lowers the weight of authority.
explanation.competitive: The role is being discounted in public.

questions.prompt: Which personal pattern best shows leadership becoming too dependent on affection?
choices: Someone holds a boundary calmly even when a few people dislike it
Someone makes every plan contingent on whether the group feels warm toward them in the moment
Someone explains a decision once and then keeps it steady

explanation.gentle: The issue is when approval becomes the real standard for leadership.
explanation.direct: That person is letting mood decide the role.

questions.prompt: Why can obvious favoritism destabilize followership?
choices: Because followers start tracking access and leverage instead of the shared mission
Because favoritism always makes a leader kinder
Because favoritism eliminates emotional reactions from the group

explanation.gentle: Visible favorites pull attention away from the work and toward who has special access.
explanation.direct: The group starts reading power through private alliances.
explanation.competitive: The room begins trading on leverage.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's distinction between authority and popularity?
choices: Authority requires total coldness, while popularity requires warmth
Authority can survive without constant liking, while popularity can weaken leadership when chased too hard
Authority and popularity are basically the same asset under pressure

explanation.gentle: Greene does not treat being liked as the same thing as leading well.
explanation.direct: A role grows weaker when it depends on repeated emotional reassurance.
explanation.competitive: Do not confuse warmth with price.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter keep distance and appearances inside the law of leadership?
choices: Because distance helps preserve symbolic weight and keeps authority from becoming too ordinary
Because distance guarantees that followers will never resent the leader
Because appearances matter more than competence or steadiness

explanation.gentle: Some form and distance can keep a role from becoming fully mood-managed.
explanation.direct: The leader should not make authority too easy to consume emotionally.

questions.prompt: How does chapter 16 connect to chapter 15 on conformity?
choices: Chapter 16 argues that once groups conform, leaders no longer matter
Chapter 16 shows that the same crowd capable of absorbing people is also unstable in how it treats leaders
Chapter 16 proves that conformity and leadership are unrelated

explanation.gentle: The crowd is powerful in both chapters, but here the focus shifts to its volatility toward authority.
explanation.direct: Group feeling does not only pull people inward; it also turns on leaders unpredictably.
explanation.competitive: The field captures hard and reprices fast.

questions.prompt: Which plan best fits the law of fickleness?
choices: Keep explaining and reopening decisions until everyone feels emotionally settled
Use coldness alone and never communicate with followers again
Lead with steadiness, avoid obvious favoritism, and stop asking the group to validate the role constantly

explanation.gentle: The chapter calls for steadiness and form, not endless bargaining or icy withdrawal.
explanation.direct: Leadership gets stronger when the role stops depending on the room for reassurance.
explanation.competitive: Hold price, cut the cheapening habits, and let the role stand.
